title: Foreign Investors Have Now Pulled More Money Out of India in 2026 Than All of Last Year. It Is Not Slowing Down.
excerpt: FPIs withdrew ₹43,000 crore in the first week of June alone, taking total outflows to ₹2.67 lakh crore — surpassing 2025's full-year exit. AI, the rupee, and a growth downgrade are all pulling in the same direction.
body:
Foreign investors pulled nearly ₹43,000 crore out of Indian equities in just the first week of June, taking total outflows for 2026 to ₹2.67 lakh crore — already surpassing the ₹1.66 lakh crore that left during the entirety of 2025.

The numbers, released by the National Securities Depository, describe something more serious than a seasonal correction. They describe a structural rotation of global capital away from India and toward the United States, driven by the gravitational pull of artificial intelligence, a weakening rupee, and a growing perception that India's earnings growth story is losing momentum.

## The Scale of the Exit

The monthly breakdown tells the story. January saw outflows of ₹35,962 crore. February offered a brief reprieve — ₹22,615 crore of inflows, the highest in 17 months. Then the floodgates opened: ₹1.17 lakh crore left in March alone, a single-month record. April added ₹60,847 crore. May contributed ₹32,963 crore. And June has started with ₹42,927 crore gone in its first five trading days.

The Sensex closed Friday at 74,243, down 116 points. The Nifty 50 settled at 23,366. Both indices moved in wide ranges — the Sensex swung over 700 points during the session — reflecting the kind of nervous, headline-driven trading that follows sustained institutional selling.

## Where the Money Is Going

Three destinations have absorbed the capital leaving India, according to Tanvi Kanchan, Associate Director at Anand Rathi: US Treasuries yielding a risk-free 4.4 per cent in dollars; gold, which has crossed $5,000 an ounce on geopolitical and inflation fears; and AI-linked equity markets in the US, Taiwan, and South Korea.

The AI factor is new and potent. The upcoming SpaceX IPO — expected to be the largest in history — along with anticipated listings from other leading AI companies, is drawing global liquidity into a handful of markets with an intensity that emerging economies simply cannot match.

"Global investors are reallocating capital towards some of the largest technology and AI-related public market opportunities currently emerging," said Rajesh Singla, founder of Alpha AMC. "This is leading to temporary capital rotation away from emerging markets, including India."

The word "temporary" may be optimistic. The Nasdaq's sharp decline on June 5 offered early signs that the AI trade might be losing steam, but even a cooling rally does not automatically redirect capital to India. Valuations have to be attractive first, and India's are not.

## The Rupee Problem

The Indian rupee has weakened nearly 6 per cent in 2026 and about 10 per cent over the past year, crossing the ₹95-per-dollar mark in May — a historic low. For foreign investors, every percentage point of rupee depreciation erodes returns earned in Indian equities, creating a vicious cycle: FPI selling weakens the rupee further, which discourages new FPI buying.

The Reserve Bank of India has responded with a battery of measures. Governor Sanjay Malhotra announced higher equity investment limits for NRIs, OCIs, and other persons resident outside India. Individual NRI limits under the Portfolio Investment Scheme are being raised from the current 5 per cent ceiling. The RBI is also absorbing hedging costs on FCNR deposits, expanding its forex swap window, and increasing access to government bonds through the Fully Accessible Route.

The Finance Ministry has exempted interest and capital gains from FPI investments in government securities from taxation — a direct attempt to lure at least some foreign capital into debt markets. Early signs suggest partial success: FPIs invested over ₹2,600 crore in debt through FAR in the first week of June, taking the year's total to ₹17,230 crore.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian American investor with exposure to Indian equities — whether through direct PIS holdings, mutual funds, or India-focused ETFs — the FPI exodus demands a clear-eyed reassessment.

The RBI's growth forecast for FY27 has been cut to 6.6 per cent from 6.9 per cent. The inflation forecast has been raised to 5.1 per cent, with a projected peak of 5.9 per cent in Q3. The repo rate stays at 5.25 per cent, but the combination of slower growth and rising prices — the early arithmetic of stagflation — narrows the central bank's room to manoeuvre.

Geojit's V K Vijayakumar put the floor condition plainly: "A sustained revival in FPI inflows will depend on a moderation in the global AI-driven investment theme." Until that happens, the smart NRI strategy may be to take advantage of the higher investment limits the RBI has just opened while being selective about entry points.

The capital fleeing India is not making a judgment about India's long-term fundamentals. It is making a judgment about where money works hardest right now. And right now, for better or worse, that place is not Dalal Street.

**Sources:** NSDL data (June 2026); The Hindu BusinessLine; Outlook Business; Livemint; RBI Monetary Policy Statement (June 5, 2026); Anand Rathi research
